## Description
Two hours from Paris and dating back to 1609, the castle is set in the centre of a woodland and the Château and its outbuildings are surrounded by a park of around fifteen hectares (pond, pastures, walled vegetable garden).
A few minutes walk from the beach and the lighthouse crossing the park, the area offers a dazzling panorama of the Alabaster coast and an exceptional view of the cliffs and the seaside.
The domain is open on the protected site, offering remarkable flora and fauna (classified as Sensitive Natural Area).
The 17th century residence can accommodate up to 150 guests in its 4 adjoining rooms: the living room, the dining room, the Galerie, the small living room. Spaces are flexible (on request), and all rooms are fully and separately equipped with high tech sound systems, to enable creating the appropriate atmosphere for each place : cocktail room, repast room, kids room & dance floor.
The capacity is not limited in the park, in the open air or in a tent / marquee. The park offers stunning views on the Channel, on the castle, and on the magnificent dovecote. The original walled vegetable garden is now a peaceful and nice grassed spot, ideal for cocktails or photo shoots.
Couples can also rely on Hélène, their dedicated bilingual hostess, to help them plan and organize the wedding of their dreams at the Chateau. The owner is experienced and certified in event planning, and she offers kind and tailored support. Depending of the fiancés' needs, services run from a simple list of recommended (but not compulsory) suppliers and accommodations*, to the full planning of an unforgettable wedding day.
The Chateau, its settings, its amenities and its people, are all dedicated to magnifying couples' best dreams of having their wedding in Normandy.
Contact the team now, and plan your free virtual tour of the domain to be 100% convinced.
*There is no on site accommodation. However, a lot of nice and quality cottages, hotels and group accommodations can be recommended in a 10-min-driving area (and taxi shuttle can be arranged). For more information please do get in touch.

## Getting there
#### Seine-Maritime
Seine-Maritime combines dramatic chalk cliffs, historic ports and beautiful Normandy countryside, creating a memorable destination for a wedding near the Channel coast.
Wedding guests can explore Rouen, walk the famous cliffs at Étretat, visit Fécamp or discover the seaside towns and beaches of the Alabaster Coast.
Fresh seafood, Normandy cheeses, cider and apple desserts provide plenty of local flavour for guests extending their stay.

## Getting there
#### Seine-Maritime
##### BY AIR
Paris 110 mins

## Location
**Normandy is one of France's most charming and diverse wedding destinations, offering everything from magnificent château wedding venues and elegant manor houses to luxury country estates and stunning coastal venues. Rich in history, natural beauty and French character, the region combines picturesque countryside, dramatic coastlines and timeless architecture, making it an outstanding choice for couples planning a destination wedding in France.**
Located just across the English Channel, Normandy is one of the easiest regions in France to reach from the UK, with convenient ferry routes, nearby airports and excellent motorway connections. Its accessibility makes it a popular destination for couples looking to bring family and friends together for a memorable wedding celebration without travelling deep into France.
The region is famous for its spectacular coastline, where dramatic cliffs, sandy beaches and charming seaside towns create breathtaking settings for ceremonies and wedding photography. The iconic white cliffs of Étretat, the elegant resorts of Deauville and Trouville, and the historic harbour of Honfleur all provide unique and romantic backdrops for unforgettable celebrations.
Away from the coast, Normandy reveals a landscape of rolling countryside, apple orchards, ancient woodlands and picturesque villages. The region is home to an impressive collection of historic châteaux, elegant manor houses and exclusive country estates, many offering private grounds, beautifully landscaped gardens and luxury accommodation for both intimate weddings and larger celebrations.
History is woven into every corner of Normandy. From the medieval city of Rouen with its magnificent cathedral to the world-famous Mont-Saint-Michel and the historic D-Day beaches, the region offers countless opportunities for guests to explore one of France's most fascinating cultural landscapes before and after your wedding.
Normandy is equally celebrated for its outstanding gastronomy. Renowned for Camembert cheese, fresh seafood, locally produced cider, Calvados and exceptional regional cuisine, the area offers couples the opportunity to create memorable wedding menus showcasing some of France's finest local produce.
Whether you're searching for a luxury château wedding venue, an exclusive country estate, a romantic coastal property, a boutique hotel or a beautifully restored manor house, Normandy offers an exceptional range of wedding venues. Many provide exclusive use, elegant reception spaces, outdoor ceremony locations, luxury accommodation and experienced wedding teams, helping ensure every celebration is as seamless as it is unforgettable.
Discover our carefully selected collection of wedding venues in Normandy and experience why this beautiful region continues to be one of France's most sought-after destinations for elegant château weddings, coastal celebrations and unforgettable destination weddings.

## Reviews
*   A truly magical exceptional place to organize all kinds of events.
Imagine: a castle which has been carefully restored, which therefore retains all of its historic charm, and which nevertheless conceals modern reception/meeting rooms, fully equipped and arranged with taste. All this in the middle of an immense domain, partly wooded, and with a view of the nearby sea. Admit that it is rather attractive!
I discovered this place during a 2-day wedding this summer. What we particularly appreciated, in addition to the framework described above, is the modularity of the places. It is possible to keep one of the rooms for meals, without changing anything in the other rooms set out for the dance floor etc. The equipment is new and of high quality. The sound system and the large flat screen are valuable for the event.
The exteriors are also very pleasant. We were able to have our reception lunch on the terrace and cocktails overlooking the sea view.
In summary, a beautiful place, conducive to serenity and an amazing venue for your wedding.   
Ines Guignard, September 2021

## Description
Two hours from Paris and dating back to 1609, the castle is set in the centre of a woodland and the Château and its outbuildings are surrounded by a park of around fifteen hectares (pond, pastures, walled vegetable garden).
A few minutes walk from the beach and the lighthouse crossing the park, the area offers a dazzling panorama of the Alabaster coast and an exceptional view of the cliffs and the seaside.
The domain is open on the protected site, offering remarkable flora and fauna (classified as Sensitive Natural Area).
The 17th century residence can accommodate up to 150 guests in its 4 adjoining rooms: the living room, the dining room, the Galerie, the small living room. Spaces are flexible (on request), and all rooms are fully and separately equipped with high tech sound systems, to enable creating the appropriate atmosphere for each place : cocktail room, repast room, kids room & dance floor.
The capacity is not limited in the park, in the open air or in a tent / marquee. The park offers stunning views on the Channel, on the castle, and on the magnificent dovecote. The original walled vegetable garden is now a peaceful and nice grassed spot, ideal for cocktails or photo shoots.
Couples can also rely on Hélène, their dedicated bilingual hostess, to help them plan and organize the wedding of their dreams at the Chateau. The owner is experienced and certified in event planning, and she offers kind and tailored support. Depending of the fiancés' needs, services run from a simple list of recommended (but not compulsory) suppliers and accommodations*, to the full planning of an unforgettable wedding day.
The Chateau, its settings, its amenities and its people, are all dedicated to magnifying couples' best dreams of having their wedding in Normandy.
Contact the team now, and plan your free virtual tour of the domain to be 100% convinced.
*There is no on site accommodation. However, a lot of nice and quality cottages, hotels and group accommodations can be recommended in a 10-min-driving area (and taxi shuttle can be arranged). For more information please do get in touch.

## Location
**Normandy is one of France's most charming and diverse wedding destinations, offering everything from magnificent château wedding venues and elegant manor houses to luxury country estates and stunning coastal venues. Rich in history, natural beauty and French character, the region combines picturesque countryside, dramatic coastlines and timeless architecture, making it an outstanding choice for couples planning a destination wedding in France.**
Located just across the English Channel, Normandy is one of the easiest regions in France to reach from the UK, with convenient ferry routes, nearby airports and excellent motorway connections. Its accessibility makes it a popular destination for couples looking to bring family and friends together for a memorable wedding celebration without travelling deep into France.
The region is famous for its spectacular coastline, where dramatic cliffs, sandy beaches and charming seaside towns create breathtaking settings for ceremonies and wedding photography. The iconic white cliffs of Étretat, the elegant resorts of Deauville and Trouville, and the historic harbour of Honfleur all provide unique and romantic backdrops for unforgettable celebrations.
Away from the coast, Normandy reveals a landscape of rolling countryside, apple orchards, ancient woodlands and picturesque villages. The region is home to an impressive collection of historic châteaux, elegant manor houses and exclusive country estates, many offering private grounds, beautifully landscaped gardens and luxury accommodation for both intimate weddings and larger celebrations.
History is woven into every corner of Normandy. From the medieval city of Rouen with its magnificent cathedral to the world-famous Mont-Saint-Michel and the historic D-Day beaches, the region offers countless opportunities for guests to explore one of France's most fascinating cultural landscapes before and after your wedding.
Normandy is equally celebrated for its outstanding gastronomy. Renowned for Camembert cheese, fresh seafood, locally produced cider, Calvados and exceptional regional cuisine, the area offers couples the opportunity to create memorable wedding menus showcasing some of France's finest local produce.
Whether you're searching for a luxury château wedding venue, an exclusive country estate, a romantic coastal property, a boutique hotel or a beautifully restored manor house, Normandy offers an exceptional range of wedding venues. Many provide exclusive use, elegant reception spaces, outdoor ceremony locations, luxury accommodation and experienced wedding teams, helping ensure every celebration is as seamless as it is unforgettable.
Discover our carefully selected collection of wedding venues in Normandy and experience why this beautiful region continues to be one of France's most sought-after destinations for elegant château weddings, coastal celebrations and unforgettable destination weddings.

*   A truly magical exceptional place to organize all kinds of events.
Imagine: a castle which has been carefully restored, which therefore retains all of its historic charm, and which nevertheless conceals modern reception/meeting rooms, fully equipped and arranged with taste. All this in the middle of an immense domain, partly wooded, and with a view of the nearby sea. Admit that it is rather attractive!
I discovered this place during a 2-day wedding this summer. What we particularly appreciated, in addition to the framework described above, is the modularity of the places. It is possible to keep one of the rooms for meals, without changing anything in the other rooms set out for the dance floor etc. The equipment is new and of high quality. The sound system and the large flat screen are valuable for the event.
The exteriors are also very pleasant. We were able to have our reception lunch on the terrace and cocktails overlooking the sea view.
In summary, a beautiful place, conducive to serenity and an amazing venue for your wedding.

#### Description
The ancient city of Korykos extends east-west alongside the highway at a distance of 65 km from Mersin and 25 km from Silifke. It sits on the slopes of the mountain where it reaches the coast. As the mountain approaches the sea, two small bays are formed. The city lies alongside northeast and southwest axis reaching Elaiussa-Sebaste at the east and Hell-Heaven Caves at the west. It is surrounded by a natural harbor, where it has been always settled around in all periods. Remains of the ancient city are spread through 113.4 ha area reaching to the northeast of modern Kızkalesi settlement and including the fullest extent of the Necropolis valley at the west and lying 2 km alongside the coast to the east.
According to Heredot, the city was founded by a Cyprian Prince namely Korykos. The name of the city was firstly recognized on the coins in the beginning of the 1st century BC when they proclaimed independency following the political unrest after the Seleuokus King Anthiokos IV death.
The first records about the property are dated back to the Hittite period but the main finds are as early as the Hellenistic period. Polygonal braided stone places on rock formations and the first city walls are remains from this period. The city was enlarged to the east in Roman period and new walls were built in the 4 th century AD, the time that the city reached the heyday. Another very important face of Korykos is its Christian period. Fourteen churches from the 4 th – 7 th centuries A.D. are preserved within this quite small area. These are located at north of the highway leading from Mersin to Silifke, just before entering the center of Kızkalesi, side by side with the Roman necropolis.
Following the Roman and early Christian period, the Byzantine and Armenian periods have to be cited, as well. Its importance as a port city continued during Byzantine times. The city was surrounded by walls again to prevent the city from the Arab attacks. Pieces of Roman period structures were used as spolia in construction of this double row city walls. The water channels built in Roman Period on the line within the Latmos Valley was rebuilt and used in early Byzantium period.

#### Description
The city was then captured by the Seljuks and Cilician Armenian Kingdom. The fortress and castle of Korykos was built on previous fortifications by the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia in the 12 th century. The castle has taken its final form in the 13th century after various additions and arrangements. The city was then sold by Armenians to Cyprus Kingdom in the 14 th century due to the attacks by Karaman Dynasty. In 1471, it was captured by the Ottomans and started to lose its importance.
As a result of this construction program, it consisted of a castle on the land, together with a castle on the sea and they formed a single defensive system. The chain between the two was pulled up in case of a threat, thus preventing enemy ships from entering the port.
The sea castle (Kızkalesi = Maiden Castle) on the small island was built on rocks at a distance of 200 meters from the shore. It was planned to prevent the bay standing in a strategic location from enemy attacks by building the sea castle as a first control point. Land castle was then constructed as a supportive defense structure. The length of the walls is 192 meters which are supported by eight towers. The entrance is provided by the north through a towered gate. There are differences in plan types of the towers which is related to the repairs held in different periods.
The land castle was built on flat ground and it had a double circuit walls covering an area that is almost square. It is surrounded by a water-filled moat. Access to the castle was provided by a bridge which could be raised or lowered over the moat and this was also the entrance to the castle. There are several square towers within the circuit walls and three chapels within the castle, but only the southeastern one is Armenian in origin, the other two chapels are Byzantine. The apse, northern wall and a section of the western wall of the Armenian Chapel are preserved.

#### Description
10 km north of the sea castle, Adamkayalar (man rocks) are placed on the rocky slopes of the Şeytan Deresi (Devils’ Valley), which are the reliefs of 11 men, 4 women, 2 children and 1 goat carved out from the rocks. This very unique place is the monumental tombs of the rulers of Korykos. However, Adamkayalar is not the only tomb of Korykos. North of the highway leadingfrom Mersin to Silifke, just before entering the center of Korykos we can observe various types of graves and tombs belonging to the Roman period. Some have the form of temple tombs, reflecting the importance of the buried person, while others are simpler, such as undecorated sarcophagi. These tombs give us an idea of how big the settlement of Korykos once was.
Villae Rusticaes (Roman Farmhouses) are other architectural components that can be seen on the site. The unique Roman type settlements, where land owner and the farm laborers live together, include crop processing and storage units, sacred places and necropolises in Korykos.

🇯🇴 Jordan

## Explore Jordan
Jordan compresses an extraordinary density of ancient history, desert wilderness, and spiritual significance into a country the size of Portugal — from the rose-red carved city of Petra in the southern highlands and the otherworldly desert of Wadi Rum to the Byzantine mosaics of Madaba, the Roman city of Jerash, and the lowest point on Earth at the Dead Sea. Aqaba's Red Sea coral reefs and the Crusader castles strung along the King's Highway add yet more dimensions to one of the Middle East's most rewarding travel itineraries. ## Most Popular
Top cities and UNESCO World Heritage Sites in Jordan.
*   1
The rose-red city of the Nabataeans is Jordan's most extraordinary sight — a vast archaeological city carved from sandstone cliffs over two millennia ago, accessible through the kilometre-long Siq gorge that suddenly opens onto the iconic Treasury facade. Beyond the Treasury, the ruins sprawl for kilometres: a colonnaded street, Royal Tombs, a Roman theatre, and the vast Monastery at the top of an 800-step climb that rewards with a view across the desert mountains to the horizon.
*   2
Jordan's capital spreads across a series of limestone hills — the old Jabal Amman and Jabal Al-Weibdeh neighbourhoods of galleries, cafés, and art spaces contrasting with the Roman Theatre and Citadel that anchor the city's ancient core. As one of the Middle East's most cosmopolitan and liveable capitals, Amman has developed a genuine dining and cultural scene that makes it a destination in its own right rather than just a base for Petra and Wadi Rum.
*   3
The Protected Area of Wadi Rum is a UNESCO Mixed Heritage site of otherworldly red-sand deserts, towering sandstone monoliths, and petroglyphs spanning 12,000 years — and the landscape made famous as the filming location for The Martian, Lawrence of Arabia, and Rogue One. Jeep tours, camel treks, and overnight stays in Bedouin camps under a canopy of stars have made this Jordan's most atmospheric and addictive wilderness experience.
*   4
Jordan's only Red Sea port sits at the tip of the Gulf of Aqaba, flanked by Saudi Arabia, Israel, and Egypt across its narrow waters, and backed by the dramatic sandstone mountains of the Jordanian desert. The reef diving here ranks among the Red Sea's finest — the Marine Peace Park protects an extraordinary array of coral and marine life — and the city's palm-fringed seafront makes it a popular winter beach escape for Amman residents.
*   5

## Most Popular
Ancient Gerasa was one of the Roman Empire's great provincial cities, and its remains — colonnaded streets, soaring Hadrian's Arch, an oval Forum, temples to Artemis and Zeus, and two well-preserved theatres — make Jerash one of the best-preserved Greco-Roman cities outside Italy. Still largely unexcavated despite its size, and bypassed by most Middle East tour itineraries in a way that makes it mercifully uncrowded relative to its magnificence.
*   6
At 430 metres below sea level — the lowest point on Earth — the Dead Sea's hyper-saline waters support no life but provide one of travel's most surreal experiences: the involuntary buoyancy that makes swimming impossible and floating inevitable. The mineral-rich black mud on the shoreline is the centrepiece of the luxury spa industry that lines the Jordanian shore, and the views across the water to the West Bank are hauntingly beautiful at dusk.
*   7
The City of Mosaics is home to the oldest surviving cartographic depiction of the Holy Land — a 6th-century Byzantine mosaic map of the Middle East covering the floor of St. George's Church — as well as dozens of other extraordinary mosaic pavements discovered beneath the modern city. Madaba is also the base for visiting Mount Nebo, where Moses is said to have looked across the Jordan River to the Promised Land he would never enter.
*   8
The great Crusader castle of Kerak — built by Pagan, lord of Transjordan, in the 1140s — commands a dramatic ridge overlooking the Dead Sea valley and is one of the largest and best-preserved Crusader fortresses in the Levant. The castle's complex history of Crusader construction, Saladin's sieges, Ayyubid modification, and eventual Mamluk expansion is written in its layered stone walls, underground passageways, and spectacular Great Hall.
*   9

## Most Popular
Qala'at Ar-Rabad — the Ajloun Castle — rises from a forested hilltop overlooking the Jordan Valley, built in 1184 by a nephew of Saladin to guard the crossing points of the Jordan River against Crusader attack. The surrounding Ajloun Forest Reserve is one of the few places in Jordan where oak, pistachio, and strawberry trees grow in dense woodland, offering some of the country's best hiking trails and views across to the hills of the West Bank.
*   10
Al-Maghtas — the UNESCO-inscribed site identified as the location of Jesus's baptism by John the Baptist — sits on the eastern bank of the Jordan River, where Byzantine and Roman churches mark the site of one of the most important events in Christian theology. The pilgrimage complex includes the actual baptism pool fed by Wadi al-Kharrar, Byzantine churches, caves where John the Baptist is said to have lived, and Elijah's Hill where the prophet is believed to have ascended to heaven.
*   11
The Wadi Mujib Biosphere Reserve — carved by the Mujib River into a canyon that plunges 900 metres from the highland plateau to the Dead Sea shore — offers some of the most exhilarating adventure hiking in the Middle East. The Siq Trail requires wading through chest-deep water between towering canyon walls; the Ibex Trail above the gorge passes through desert mountain terrain where Nubian ibex pick their way along the ledges.
*   12
Ancient Gadara sits on a basalt plateau in the far north of Jordan, its black-stone colonnaded streets and Roman theatre looking out over the Sea of Galilee, the Golan Heights, and the Jordan River valley in a panorama that takes in four countries on a clear day. Less visited than Jerash but arguably more dramatic in its setting, Umm Qais was one of the ancient Decapolis cities and is mentioned in the Gospel of Mark as the location of Jesus's healing of two demoniacs.
*   13

## Most Popular
The village of Dana clings to the edge of the Wadi Dana escarpment in a location so dramatic — perched on the rim of Jordan's largest nature reserve with the canyon dropping away below — that simply arriving is an event. Dana Biosphere Reserve protects four distinct ecosystems ranging from 1,500-metre sandstone peaks to the arid depths of Wadi Araba, and is one of the best places in Jordan to spot Nubian ibex, sand cats, wolves, and over 200 bird species.
*   14
The UNESCO World Heritage city of As-Salt was once the most important commercial and administrative centre in Transjordan, its lanes of beautifully preserved Ottoman-era stone mansions built in distinctive yellow limestone with arched windows and ornamental ironwork. The city's multicultural history of Ottoman administrators, Christian merchants, and Muslim notables living in close quarters is reflected in churches and mosques standing side by side in the old centre.
*   15
The castle of Montreal — Shobak — was the first Crusader fortress built in Transjordan, established by Baldwin I of Jerusalem in 1115 on a conical hill rising from the desert plateau south of the Dead Sea. Less visited than Kerak and all the more rewarding for it, Shobak's skeletal towers and a secret tunnel carved through the rock to a spring 375 steps below the castle floor give a more evocative sense of Crusader life than any other site in the country.
* * *

## The Traveller's Jordan
Every Jordan itinerary has one non-negotiable: Petra. The approach through the Siq — a kilometre-long gorge whose walls narrow to almost touching before the carved facade of the Treasury appears at the end like a stage set — has been repeated tens of thousands of times, and still works. The city beyond it is vast and mostly unexcavated, sprawling across a series of wadis with its own colonnaded street, Byzantine church, Nabataean high places, and the Monastery an exhausting 850 steps above the main site. Give it two days if you can. Wadi Rum, three hours further south, operates on an entirely different register: the silence and scale of the red-sand desert, best experienced sleeping in a Bedouin camp under a sky with no light pollution whatsoever, has a way of resetting priorities.
The north of the country offers a different Jordan entirely. Jerash — ancient Gerasa — is often called the Pompeii of the Middle East, and the comparison is apt: its colonnaded cardo, oval forum, and two theatres are more intact than most Roman cities in Italy, and it receives a fraction of the visitors. Madaba, an hour south of Amman, contains the oldest surviving map of the Holy Land — a 6th-century Byzantine mosaic floor you walk around rather than through — and is the base for the short drive to Mount Nebo. The Dead Sea is as much an experience as a destination: once you've floated in its hyper-saline water reading a newspaper, you will understand why every travel brochure has been making the same joke for 50 years. And Aqaba, at the tip of the Gulf, offers some of the finest Red Sea diving accessible by land — the Marine Peace Park's reefs are pristine and largely uncrowded compared to their counterparts across the water in Egypt. **How many have you made it to?**
* * *

## Practical Travel Facts
🏛️Capital Amman Jordan's largest city sprawls across seven (now many more) limestone hills and serves as the country's main international gateway — Queen Alia International Airport is 35 km south of the city centre.
💰Currency Jordanian Dinar (JOD / JD)1 JOD ≈ $1.41 USD — the dinar is one of the highest-valued currencies in the world. US dollars are not accepted for most purchases; exchange on arrival or use ATMs.
🗣️Languages Arabic Arabic is the sole official language; English is widely spoken in hotels, restaurants, and tourist sites throughout the country, making Jordan one of the most accessible Arabic-speaking destinations for Western visitors.
🔌Power Type C + D + F + G · 230 V · 50 Hz Jordan uses a mix of socket types; Type G (British square-pin) is common in hotels. US visitors need both an adapter and a voltage converter for non-dual-voltage devices.
📞Dialing Code+962 Dial +962 then drop the leading 0 from the local number. Local SIM cards (Zain, Orange, Umniah) are cheap and widely available at the airport.
🕐Time Zone AST · UTC+3 Jordan abolished daylight saving time in 2022 and now stays on UTC+3 year-round — no seasonal clock change.
🚗Driving Side Right Roads between major sites are generally well-maintained; the King's Highway and Desert Highway connect Amman to Petra and Aqaba. Driving in Amman itself can be chaotic — take taxis or rideshares in the city.
💧Tap Water Bottled only Tap water varies widely by area and is not recommended for tourists. Bottled water costs under $1/litre and is available everywhere — including at Petra and Wadi Rum camps.
🧾Tipping Expected 10% is standard in restaurants; service charges on the bill often don't reach the wait staff, so tip in cash directly. Guides and drivers also expect a tip at the end of the day.
🛡️Safety Exercise caution Jordan maintains a US State Department Level 2 advisory (exercise increased caution) due to regional tensions. Internal crime is low; avoid border areas with Syria and Iraq. Jordan itself is considered one of the safer countries in the Middle East for tourists.

## Practical Travel Facts
🍽️Food & Drink Mansaf · Maqluba · Falafel · Kanafeh · Mint tea Mansaf — lamb slow-cooked in fermented dried yoghurt (jameed) served over rice — is the national dish, eaten at celebrations. Kanafeh, the warm cheese-and-pastry dessert drenched in syrup, is the essential sweet.
⛷️Sport Football · Basketball Football is the most popular spectator sport; the Jordanian national team has qualified for the AFC Asian Cup. Adventure activities — hiking Wadi Rum, canyoning in Wadi Mujib, diving Aqaba — are the country's main active tourism draw.
🗓️Best Time to Visit Mar–May; Oct–Nov Spring and autumn offer mild temperatures for Petra (hot in summer, cold at night in winter) and comfortable Wadi Rum camping. January is good for uncrowded historical sites; July–August is very hot in the desert interior.
💸Budget Mid-range Jordan is not cheap by regional standards — Petra entry alone is JOD 50 ($70), and Wadi Rum camps range from budget to very expensive. Daily costs are lower than Israel or the Gulf states but higher than Egypt.
✈️Visa Visa on arrival / Jordan Pass Most Western nationals (US, UK, EU, Canada, Australia) obtain a single-entry visa on arrival for JOD 40 (~$56). The Jordan Pass bundles the visa with Petra admission and other sites — recommended for most visitors.

About seven miles south of the Lake of Galilee is the only bridge across Jordan which is now in use. It is called _Jier Mejamî'a_ (Mejamî'a bridge), and is the crossing-place for caravans from Beisan', Nab'lus, and all the region south of those places, to Damascus. After crossing here, the road follows the Jordan Valley for a few miles, and then turns up into the hills. This bridge is built entirely of blocks of basalt, and consists of one long arch spanning the river and three smaller ones on the eastern side, to allow the passage of the overflow when the river is out of its ordinary banks. The floor of the bridge is not level, as if intended for vehicles, but it climbs the arch, and has steps going up one side and down the other, each step about eight inches high.
It was evidently not built for vehicles, though strong ones could be drawn over it with proper care. A short distance from it on the western bank is a dilapidated khân, which once answered the double purpose of a halting-place for caravans and a military post for the protection of travelers. Just below the bridge there is an almost perpendicular descent of the river, with a fall of 10 or 12 feet. The current is fearfully rapid, and is lashed into foam by projecting rocks. Above, there is deep, still water and a broad channel.

A mile and a half above this bridge is the mouth of the River Yar'mûk (page 34), across which, a few miles above its mouth, but after it has entered the Jordan Plain, is a bridge for the passage of the Damascus road, mentioned above. On the northern bank of this river, three miles above its entrance into the Jordan Valley, are the [354]  celebrated hot springs called by the natives El Ham'mâ. They are in a valley three-quarters of a mile wide, and are four in number. The largest occupies a basin 180 feet long by 90 in width, in which the water stands 6 feet deep, with a temperature of 103°. The overflow from it makes a pond, in a low place, 100 yards long, 10 or 15 wide, and 10 feet deep. The combined streams flowing from all these springs are estimated by Dr. Merrill as equal to a stream 21 feet wide and 20 inches deep, with a swift current. The waters are impregnated with sulphur and other minerals, and have healthy properties. Imposing ruins are scattered about them,--the remains of bath-houses and dwellings,--all of basalt. "If El Ham'mâ could be rebuilt," says Dr. Merrill, "it would be one of the most attractive resorts in Syria, and perhaps in the world."42
The Jordan Valley above the mouth of the Yar'mûk to the southern end of the lake has a rich, reddish soil, is well cultivated, and very productive. That on the western side of the river, from the Mejamî'a Bridge upward, is narrow and broken, but it has many small fields of rich soil, and several villages perched on the tops of hills. The ruins of five bridges are seen in this section of the river, although the river is fordable at many places the greater part of the year.
We have now completed our view of the topography of the Jordan Valley, and the reader can readily see that the eastern half of it, though almost entirely unknown until within the last ten years, is by far the more interesting, both for its natural resources and its remains of antiquity.
§ III.
IN THE UPLANDS BEYOND THE JORDAN.

The number of localities beyond the Jordan which are mentioned in the Scriptures is surprisingly small, and of the few which are mentioned the accounts given are very meagre. Yet the number of cities and towns of which well-preserved and imposing ruins are left is greater in proportion to the territory than in the better-known country west of the river. There is also this remarkable difference, that the sites of the ancient cities west of the Jordan are still inhabited, and their ruins have been utilized in the construction of the present habitations, while those beyond the river are nearly all totally deserted, and remain as they were left by their ancient inhabitants. As our [355]  purpose in this work is to limit our attention almost exclusively to places which have a Bible history, we can only glance at many places which would otherwise demand careful description. We begin with the more northern portion, called the Haurân' by the Ar'abs, but known in the Old Testament period as Ba'shan.
We have stated in § II. that the Mejamî'a Bridge, seven miles south of the Lake of Galilee, is the crossing-place for the road from Southern Palestine to Damascus. It was doubtless at this bridge that
RUINS OF GAD'ARA.
Naaman the Syrian crossed on his way from Damascus to Samaria to see the prophet and it was most likely in the river at this point that he dipped himself seven times in the Jordan in order to be healed of the leprosy.43 It was here, too, that Paul crossed on his way to Damascus as a persecutor,44 and it will be convenient for us to follow his route for a short distance in reaching the places to be described in this section.

Following the road from the bridge just mentioned up the Jordan [356]  Valley to the Yar'mûk, crossing the river on the stone bridge which spans it, and then ascending the bank of the river to the hot springs, we reach the limit in this direction of the topography given in § II. About three miles farther up the Yar'mûk, and on its southern bank, are the ruins of Gad'ara, now called Mkês. It is situated on the western extremity of a mountain crest which stands between the Yar'mûk on the north and a deep wâdy on the south. Many heaps of hewn stones and fragments of broken columns whose capitals were of the Corinthian order are scattered about over a large space. The street pavement of basalt is preserved in many places, and is marked by the ruts of the chariot-wheels. Two theatres are found among the ruins, one of them in a good state of preservation. The principal street had a row of columns on either side, all of which are now broken. The cut on the opposite page gives a view of a part of this street, and of one of the theatres.
East of the city is the ancient cemetery, where there are many rock-cut tombs, and where as many as 200 stone sarcophagi have been counted. The city was built of basalt, which is the prevailing rock in all this region. The ruins are principally of the Roman period, very little that is Jewish being now discernible. Gad'ara was the chief city of the district called Decapolis,45 which lay to the southwest of the Lake of Galilee, and the land of the Gergesenes, on the eastern shore of that lake, was included in the territory belonging to the Gadarenes.46

About eight miles in an air-line due north of Gad'ara, and on the summit of the hills east of the Lake of Galilee, is the ancient city of A'phek, now called Fîk. It was here that Ahab, king of Israel, gained a signal victory over Benhadad, king of Syria, and where 27,000 of the men of the latter perished as the result of the falling of the city-wall.47 It is now a well-watered caravan-station on a more westward branch of the Damascus road, and is reached by following that road direct from the Mejamî'a bridge, but it has no important remains of antiquity.
The road by which we reach Gad'ara from the Jordan Valley continues up the valley of the river Yar'mûk in a course a little north of east until it intersects at Mzerîb the great pilgrim route from Damascus to Mecca. It requires nearly ten hours to make the journey over the [357]  rough and crooked road, but in an air-line it is less than twenty miles between the two places. Mzerîb is one of the principal halting-places of the vast caravans of Mohammedan pilgrims who assemble every spring at Damascus and make the pilgrimage thence to Mecca, a journey of 27 days. The place is well watered by a large spring, and it is supplied with a very large castle for the protection of the caravans in times of lawlessness.
From Mzerîb to Damascus along the pilgrim road is about 45 miles. This route is not often followed by travelers, on account of the danger--real or imaginary--of being robbed on the way, but it is the route followed by Paul on his journey to Damascus, and the one on which an attempt has been made to fix the spot at which he was confronted by that vision from heaven which turned the tide of his life. But the account in the Scriptures is too indefinite to enable one to fix the spot with any near approach to accuracy.48

Among the sixty walled cities taken by Moses from Og, king of Ba'shan, only three are mentioned by name, and one of these is Salcah.54 As you stand on the castle or on the minaret at Bozrah and look due east, you see Salcah, about 12 miles distant, crowning a conical eminence 500 feet high. Between the two there is a Roman road as straight as an arrow over the level plain, with some of its pavement in a good state of preservation. The name of this very ancient city is preserved with only the slight change to Salchâd'. The approach to the walls on the summit of the hill is guarded by two deep moats, one higher up than the other, and in the days of its glory the city must have been well-nigh impregnable. The ruins are massive, and from their highest walls a magnificent view of the surrounding country is obtained. Eastward is the boundless desert, reaching off to the Euphra'tes; toward the southwest are the high mountains which overhang the lower Jordan; to the northwest is Mount Hermon; to the north are the lofts and rugged mountains of the Haurân'; while all around at short distances are a multitude of ruined cities which speak mournfully of departed glory. Armies and earthquakes, guided by an avenging Providence, have wrought this ruin.
If we leave Bozrah by the road leading to the north, we pass some town or city with interesting ruins every four or five miles, and at a distance of about 20 miles we reach Kûnawât', a ruined city on the [360]
A PALACE IN KÛAWÂT'.  
Page 361.

western slope of the Haurân' mountains. It is built on both sides of a stream which descends from the mountain, and it extends along the stream about a mile and a half. It is supposed to be the Ke'nath mentioned in Numbers (xxxii. 42) as having been occupied by a portion of the tribe of Manasseh, and, although that tribe could scarcely have extended their settlements so far north, the name tends to confirm the identification. Kûnawât' is equally remarkable with Bozrah for the extent and magnificence of its ruins, and what we have said of the former might almost be repeated of the latter. The cut on the opposite page presents a view of only one among its many ruined edifices, and only one of several views of the same building that are equally imposing.
In this city are found many well-preserved houses built entirely of stone, even to the door-shutters. The walls were built without cement, the stones in some instances being "dove-tailed," and in some instances cut with projections on top to fit into corresponding depressions in the bottom of those next above, so as to prevent them from slipping. The floors are made of slabs or of the natural rock artificially leveled, and the ceilings and roofs of thick slabs of stone long enough to reach from wall to wall, with their joints closed by cement. The door is a smoothly-dressed slab of sufficient width and height, and its hinges are projecting points at the top and bottom on one side, which fit in sockets made for them in the sill and lintel. They vary in thickness from 8 to 12 inches, and sometimes there are two slabs to an entrance, making a folding-door. It was no easy task to open such doors; but we are not to think of the children running in and out and slamming the doors behind them every minute in the day. They probably stood open day and night, except when danger from burglars required them to be closed, and in that case it is clear that burglars' tools were not of much service. Such doors are found in all the rocky regions of the Haurân' and the Lejâh'.

About seven miles south of the Lake of Galilee is the only bridge across Jordan which is now in use. It is called _Jier Mejamî'a_ (Mejamî'a bridge), and is the crossing-place for caravans from Beisan', Nab'lus, and all the region south of those places, to Damascus. After crossing here, the road follows the Jordan Valley for a few miles, and then turns up into the hills. This bridge is built entirely of blocks of basalt, and consists of one long arch spanning the river and three smaller ones on the eastern side, to allow the passage of the overflow when the river is out of its ordinary banks. The floor of the bridge is not level, as if intended for vehicles, but it climbs the arch, and has steps going up one side and down the other, each step about eight inches high.
It was evidently not built for vehicles, though strong ones could be drawn over it with proper care. A short distance from it on the western bank is a dilapidated khân, which once answered the double purpose of a halting-place for caravans and a military post for the protection of travelers. Just below the bridge there is an almost perpendicular descent of the river, with a fall of 10 or 12 feet. The current is fearfully rapid, and is lashed into foam by projecting rocks. Above, there is deep, still water and a broad channel.

A mile and a half above this bridge is the mouth of the River Yar'mûk (page 34), across which, a few miles above its mouth, but after it has entered the Jordan Plain, is a bridge for the passage of the Damascus road, mentioned above. On the northern bank of this river, three miles above its entrance into the Jordan Valley, are the [354]  celebrated hot springs called by the natives El Ham'mâ. They are in a valley three-quarters of a mile wide, and are four in number. The largest occupies a basin 180 feet long by 90 in width, in which the water stands 6 feet deep, with a temperature of 103°. The overflow from it makes a pond, in a low place, 100 yards long, 10 or 15 wide, and 10 feet deep. The combined streams flowing from all these springs are estimated by Dr. Merrill as equal to a stream 21 feet wide and 20 inches deep, with a swift current. The waters are impregnated with sulphur and other minerals, and have healthy properties. Imposing ruins are scattered about them,--the remains of bath-houses and dwellings,--all of basalt. "If El Ham'mâ could be rebuilt," says Dr. Merrill, "it would be one of the most attractive resorts in Syria, and perhaps in the world."42
The Jordan Valley above the mouth of the Yar'mûk to the southern end of the lake has a rich, reddish soil, is well cultivated, and very productive. That on the western side of the river, from the Mejamî'a Bridge upward, is narrow and broken, but it has many small fields of rich soil, and several villages perched on the tops of hills. The ruins of five bridges are seen in this section of the river, although the river is fordable at many places the greater part of the year.
We have now completed our view of the topography of the Jordan Valley, and the reader can readily see that the eastern half of it, though almost entirely unknown until within the last ten years, is by far the more interesting, both for its natural resources and its remains of antiquity.
§ III.
IN THE UPLANDS BEYOND THE JORDAN.

The number of localities beyond the Jordan which are mentioned in the Scriptures is surprisingly small, and of the few which are mentioned the accounts given are very meagre. Yet the number of cities and towns of which well-preserved and imposing ruins are left is greater in proportion to the territory than in the better-known country west of the river. There is also this remarkable difference, that the sites of the ancient cities west of the Jordan are still inhabited, and their ruins have been utilized in the construction of the present habitations, while those beyond the river are nearly all totally deserted, and remain as they were left by their ancient inhabitants. As our [355]  purpose in this work is to limit our attention almost exclusively to places which have a Bible history, we can only glance at many places which would otherwise demand careful description. We begin with the more northern portion, called the Haurân' by the Ar'abs, but known in the Old Testament period as Ba'shan.
We have stated in § II. that the Mejamî'a Bridge, seven miles south of the Lake of Galilee, is the crossing-place for the road from Southern Palestine to Damascus. It was doubtless at this bridge that
RUINS OF GAD'ARA.
Naaman the Syrian crossed on his way from Damascus to Samaria to see the prophet and it was most likely in the river at this point that he dipped himself seven times in the Jordan in order to be healed of the leprosy.43 It was here, too, that Paul crossed on his way to Damascus as a persecutor,44 and it will be convenient for us to follow his route for a short distance in reaching the places to be described in this section.

Following the road from the bridge just mentioned up the Jordan [356]  Valley to the Yar'mûk, crossing the river on the stone bridge which spans it, and then ascending the bank of the river to the hot springs, we reach the limit in this direction of the topography given in § II. About three miles farther up the Yar'mûk, and on its southern bank, are the ruins of Gad'ara, now called Mkês. It is situated on the western extremity of a mountain crest which stands between the Yar'mûk on the north and a deep wâdy on the south. Many heaps of hewn stones and fragments of broken columns whose capitals were of the Corinthian order are scattered about over a large space. The street pavement of basalt is preserved in many places, and is marked by the ruts of the chariot-wheels. Two theatres are found among the ruins, one of them in a good state of preservation. The principal street had a row of columns on either side, all of which are now broken. The cut on the opposite page gives a view of a part of this street, and of one of the theatres.
East of the city is the ancient cemetery, where there are many rock-cut tombs, and where as many as 200 stone sarcophagi have been counted. The city was built of basalt, which is the prevailing rock in all this region. The ruins are principally of the Roman period, very little that is Jewish being now discernible. Gad'ara was the chief city of the district called Decapolis,45 which lay to the southwest of the Lake of Galilee, and the land of the Gergesenes, on the eastern shore of that lake, was included in the territory belonging to the Gadarenes.46

About eight miles in an air-line due north of Gad'ara, and on the summit of the hills east of the Lake of Galilee, is the ancient city of A'phek, now called Fîk. It was here that Ahab, king of Israel, gained a signal victory over Benhadad, king of Syria, and where 27,000 of the men of the latter perished as the result of the falling of the city-wall.47 It is now a well-watered caravan-station on a more westward branch of the Damascus road, and is reached by following that road direct from the Mejamî'a bridge, but it has no important remains of antiquity.
The road by which we reach Gad'ara from the Jordan Valley continues up the valley of the river Yar'mûk in a course a little north of east until it intersects at Mzerîb the great pilgrim route from Damascus to Mecca. It requires nearly ten hours to make the journey over the [357]  rough and crooked road, but in an air-line it is less than twenty miles between the two places. Mzerîb is one of the principal halting-places of the vast caravans of Mohammedan pilgrims who assemble every spring at Damascus and make the pilgrimage thence to Mecca, a journey of 27 days. The place is well watered by a large spring, and it is supplied with a very large castle for the protection of the caravans in times of lawlessness.
From Mzerîb to Damascus along the pilgrim road is about 45 miles. This route is not often followed by travelers, on account of the danger--real or imaginary--of being robbed on the way, but it is the route followed by Paul on his journey to Damascus, and the one on which an attempt has been made to fix the spot at which he was confronted by that vision from heaven which turned the tide of his life. But the account in the Scriptures is too indefinite to enable one to fix the spot with any near approach to accuracy.48

Among the sixty walled cities taken by Moses from Og, king of Ba'shan, only three are mentioned by name, and one of these is Salcah.54 As you stand on the castle or on the minaret at Bozrah and look due east, you see Salcah, about 12 miles distant, crowning a conical eminence 500 feet high. Between the two there is a Roman road as straight as an arrow over the level plain, with some of its pavement in a good state of preservation. The name of this very ancient city is preserved with only the slight change to Salchâd'. The approach to the walls on the summit of the hill is guarded by two deep moats, one higher up than the other, and in the days of its glory the city must have been well-nigh impregnable. The ruins are massive, and from their highest walls a magnificent view of the surrounding country is obtained. Eastward is the boundless desert, reaching off to the Euphra'tes; toward the southwest are the high mountains which overhang the lower Jordan; to the northwest is Mount Hermon; to the north are the lofts and rugged mountains of the Haurân'; while all around at short distances are a multitude of ruined cities which speak mournfully of departed glory. Armies and earthquakes, guided by an avenging Providence, have wrought this ruin.
If we leave Bozrah by the road leading to the north, we pass some town or city with interesting ruins every four or five miles, and at a distance of about 20 miles we reach Kûnawât', a ruined city on the [360]
A PALACE IN KÛAWÂT'.  
Page 361.
texts.32:
western slope of the Haurân' mountains. It is built on both sides of a stream which descends from the mountain, and it extends along the stream about a mile and a half. It is supposed to be the Ke'nath mentioned in Numbers (xxxii. 42) as having been occupied by a portion of the tribe of Manasseh, and, although that tribe could scarcely have extended their settlements so far north, the name tends to confirm the identification. Kûnawât' is equally remarkable with Bozrah for the extent and magnificence of its ruins, and what we have said of the former might almost be repeated of the latter. The cut on the opposite page presents a view of only one among its many ruined edifices, and only one of several views of the same building that are equally imposing.
In this city are found many well-preserved houses built entirely of stone, even to the door-shutters. The walls were built without cement, the stones in some instances being "dove-tailed," and in some instances cut with projections on top to fit into corresponding depressions in the bottom of those next above, so as to prevent them from slipping. The floors are made of slabs or of the natural rock artificially leveled, and the ceilings and roofs of thick slabs of stone long enough to reach from wall to wall, with their joints closed by cement. The door is a smoothly-dressed slab of sufficient width and height, and its hinges are projecting points at the top and bottom on one side, which fit in sockets made for them in the sill and lintel. They vary in thickness from 8 to 12 inches, and sometimes there are two slabs to an entrance, making a folding-door. It was no easy task to open such doors; but we are not to think of the children running in and out and slamming the doors behind them every minute in the day. They probably stood open day and night, except when danger from burglars required them to be closed, and in that case it is clear that burglars' tools were not of much service. Such doors are found in all the rocky regions of the Haurân' and the Lejâh'.

Jordan compresses an extraordinary density of ancient history, desert wilderness, and spiritual significance into a country the size of Portugal — from the rose-red carved city of Petra in the southern highlands and the otherworldly desert of Wadi Rum to the Byzantine mosaics of Madaba, the Roman city of Jerash, and the lowest point on Earth at the Dead Sea. Aqaba's Red Sea coral reefs and the Crusader castles strung along the King's Highway add yet more dimensions to one of the Middle East's most rewarding travel itineraries. ## Most Popular
Top cities and UNESCO World Heritage Sites in Jordan.
*   1
The rose-red city of the Nabataeans is Jordan's most extraordinary sight — a vast archaeological city carved from sandstone cliffs over two millennia ago, accessible through the kilometre-long Siq gorge that suddenly opens onto the iconic Treasury facade. Beyond the Treasury, the ruins sprawl for kilometres: a colonnaded street, Royal Tombs, a Roman theatre, and the vast Monastery at the top of an 800-step climb that rewards with a view across the desert mountains to the horizon.
*   2
Jordan's capital spreads across a series of limestone hills — the old Jabal Amman and Jabal Al-Weibdeh neighbourhoods of galleries, cafés, and art spaces contrasting with the Roman Theatre and Citadel that anchor the city's ancient core. As one of the Middle East's most cosmopolitan and liveable capitals, Amman has developed a genuine dining and cultural scene that makes it a destination in its own right rather than just a base for Petra and Wadi Rum.
*   3
The Protected Area of Wadi Rum is a UNESCO Mixed Heritage site of otherworldly red-sand deserts, towering sandstone monoliths, and petroglyphs spanning 12,000 years — and the landscape made famous as the filming location for The Martian, Lawrence of Arabia, and Rogue One. Jeep tours, camel treks, and overnight stays in Bedouin camps under a canopy of stars have made this Jordan's most atmospheric and addictive wilderness experience.
*   4
Jordan's only Red Sea port sits at the tip of the Gulf of Aqaba, flanked by Saudi Arabia, Israel, and Egypt across its narrow waters, and backed by the dramatic sandstone mountains of the Jordanian desert. The reef diving here ranks among the Red Sea's finest — the Marine Peace Park protects an extraordinary array of coral and marine life — and the city's palm-fringed seafront makes it a popular winter beach escape for Amman residents.
*   5
texts.3:
## Most Popular
Ancient Gerasa was one of the Roman Empire's great provincial cities, and its remains — colonnaded streets, soaring Hadrian's Arch, an oval Forum, temples to Artemis and Zeus, and two well-preserved theatres — make Jerash one of the best-preserved Greco-Roman cities outside Italy. Still largely unexcavated despite its size, and bypassed by most Middle East tour itineraries in a way that makes it mercifully uncrowded relative to its magnificence.
*   6
At 430 metres below sea level — the lowest point on Earth — the Dead Sea's hyper-saline waters support no life but provide one of travel's most surreal experiences: the involuntary buoyancy that makes swimming impossible and floating inevitable. The mineral-rich black mud on the shoreline is the centrepiece of the luxury spa industry that lines the Jordanian shore, and the views across the water to the West Bank are hauntingly beautiful at dusk.
*   7
The City of Mosaics is home to the oldest surviving cartographic depiction of the Holy Land — a 6th-century Byzantine mosaic map of the Middle East covering the floor of St. George's Church — as well as dozens of other extraordinary mosaic pavements discovered beneath the modern city. Madaba is also the base for visiting Mount Nebo, where Moses is said to have looked across the Jordan River to the Promised Land he would never enter.
*   8
The great Crusader castle of Kerak — built by Pagan, lord of Transjordan, in the 1140s — commands a dramatic ridge overlooking the Dead Sea valley and is one of the largest and best-preserved Crusader fortresses in the Levant. The castle's complex history of Crusader construction, Saladin's sieges, Ayyubid modification, and eventual Mamluk expansion is written in its layered stone walls, underground passageways, and spectacular Great Hall.
*   9
texts.4:
## Most Popular
Qala'at Ar-Rabad — the Ajloun Castle — rises from a forested hilltop overlooking the Jordan Valley, built in 1184 by a nephew of Saladin to guard the crossing points of the Jordan River against Crusader attack. The surrounding Ajloun Forest Reserve is one of the few places in Jordan where oak, pistachio, and strawberry trees grow in dense woodland, offering some of the country's best hiking trails and views across to the hills of the West Bank.
*   10
Al-Maghtas — the UNESCO-inscribed site identified as the location of Jesus's baptism by John the Baptist — sits on the eastern bank of the Jordan River, where Byzantine and Roman churches mark the site of one of the most important events in Christian theology. The pilgrimage complex includes the actual baptism pool fed by Wadi al-Kharrar, Byzantine churches, caves where John the Baptist is said to have lived, and Elijah's Hill where the prophet is believed to have ascended to heaven.
*   11
The Wadi Mujib Biosphere Reserve — carved by the Mujib River into a canyon that plunges 900 metres from the highland plateau to the Dead Sea shore — offers some of the most exhilarating adventure hiking in the Middle East. The Siq Trail requires wading through chest-deep water between towering canyon walls; the Ibex Trail above the gorge passes through desert mountain terrain where Nubian ibex pick their way along the ledges.
*   12
Ancient Gadara sits on a basalt plateau in the far north of Jordan, its black-stone colonnaded streets and Roman theatre looking out over the Sea of Galilee, the Golan Heights, and the Jordan River valley in a panorama that takes in four countries on a clear day. Less visited than Jerash but arguably more dramatic in its setting, Umm Qais was one of the ancient Decapolis cities and is mentioned in the Gospel of Mark as the location of Jesus's healing of two demoniacs.
*   13
texts.5:
## Most Popular
The village of Dana clings to the edge of the Wadi Dana escarpment in a location so dramatic — perched on the rim of Jordan's largest nature reserve with the canyon dropping away below — that simply arriving is an event. Dana Biosphere Reserve protects four distinct ecosystems ranging from 1,500-metre sandstone peaks to the arid depths of Wadi Araba, and is one of the best places in Jordan to spot Nubian ibex, sand cats, wolves, and over 200 bird species.
*   14
The UNESCO World Heritage city of As-Salt was once the most important commercial and administrative centre in Transjordan, its lanes of beautifully preserved Ottoman-era stone mansions built in distinctive yellow limestone with arched windows and ornamental ironwork. The city's multicultural history of Ottoman administrators, Christian merchants, and Muslim notables living in close quarters is reflected in churches and mosques standing side by side in the old centre.
*   15
The castle of Montreal — Shobak — was the first Crusader fortress built in Transjordan, established by Baldwin I of Jerusalem in 1115 on a conical hill rising from the desert plateau south of the Dead Sea. Less visited than Kerak and all the more rewarding for it, Shobak's skeletal towers and a secret tunnel carved through the rock to a spring 375 steps below the castle floor give a more evocative sense of Crusader life than any other site in the country.
* * *
texts.6:
## The Traveller's Jordan
Every Jordan itinerary has one non-negotiable: Petra. The approach through the Siq — a kilometre-long gorge whose walls narrow to almost touching before the carved facade of the Treasury appears at the end like a stage set — has been repeated tens of thousands of times, and still works. The city beyond it is vast and mostly unexcavated, sprawling across a series of wadis with its own colonnaded street, Byzantine church, Nabataean high places, and the Monastery an exhausting 850 steps above the main site. Give it two days if you can. Wadi Rum, three hours further south, operates on an entirely different register: the silence and scale of the red-sand desert, best experienced sleeping in a Bedouin camp under a sky with no light pollution whatsoever, has a way of resetting priorities.
The north of the country offers a different Jordan entirely. Jerash — ancient Gerasa — is often called the Pompeii of the Middle East, and the comparison is apt: its colonnaded cardo, oval forum, and two theatres are more intact than most Roman cities in Italy, and it receives a fraction of the visitors. Madaba, an hour south of Amman, contains the oldest surviving map of the Holy Land — a 6th-century Byzantine mosaic floor you walk around rather than through — and is the base for the short drive to Mount Nebo. The Dead Sea is as much an experience as a destination: once you've floated in its hyper-saline water reading a newspaper, you will understand why every travel brochure has been making the same joke for 50 years. And Aqaba, at the tip of the Gulf, offers some of the finest Red Sea diving accessible by land — the Marine Peace Park's reefs are pristine and largely uncrowded compared to their counterparts across the water in Egypt. **How many have you made it to?**
* * *

## Practical Travel Facts
🏛️Capital Amman Jordan's largest city sprawls across seven (now many more) limestone hills and serves as the country's main international gateway — Queen Alia International Airport is 35 km south of the city centre.
💰Currency Jordanian Dinar (JOD / JD)1 JOD ≈ $1.41 USD — the dinar is one of the highest-valued currencies in the world. US dollars are not accepted for most purchases; exchange on arrival or use ATMs.
🗣️Languages Arabic Arabic is the sole official language; English is widely spoken in hotels, restaurants, and tourist sites throughout the country, making Jordan one of the most accessible Arabic-speaking destinations for Western visitors.
🔌Power Type C + D + F + G · 230 V · 50 Hz Jordan uses a mix of socket types; Type G (British square-pin) is common in hotels. US visitors need both an adapter and a voltage converter for non-dual-voltage devices.
📞Dialing Code+962 Dial +962 then drop the leading 0 from the local number. Local SIM cards (Zain, Orange, Umniah) are cheap and widely available at the airport.
🕐Time Zone AST · UTC+3 Jordan abolished daylight saving time in 2022 and now stays on UTC+3 year-round — no seasonal clock change.
🚗Driving Side Right Roads between major sites are generally well-maintained; the King's Highway and Desert Highway connect Amman to Petra and Aqaba. Driving in Amman itself can be chaotic — take taxis or rideshares in the city.

View across Charles Bridge to the Prague Castle ()
Plenty of films have been shot across Europe, but iconic castles are hard to miss. Here are some incredible castle filming locations that you can visit.
**Schloss Waldenburg, Germany**
Castle (Schloss) Waldenburg, in Saxony, has one of the moodiest, most authentic wood paneled interiors from medieval Europe. It has been used for numerous German period films and shows, but you may recognize it best for its use in “The Grand Budapest Hotel.” In the film, the dark hallways, staircases and parlors of Madame Desgoffe-und-Taxi’s (Tilda Swinton) Schloss Lutz were filmed in the interior of Castle Waldenburg. When young Gustave (Ralph Fiennes) and Zero (Tony Revlori) steal the painting, it is from above the fireplace in Waldenburg’s shadowy library.
Castle Waldenburg was built in the 1100s and has undergone numerous updates and remodeling since that time. The town and castle were ruled over by the Hohenlohe dynasty, who’s descendent, Prince Felix zu Hohenlohe-Waldenburg-Schillingsfürst, still owns the property. Inside the castle are museum spaces dedicated to its history. In addition, there are two restaurants on the grounds offering both café fare and fine dining. When not in use for events or film projects, the interior rooms of the castle can be toured with an informational app. You can also do a virtual tour on the website at www.schloss-waldenburg.de.
Schloss Waldenburg interior (Martin Geisler, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons)
**Schloss Frohnburg, Austria**
Situated on the southern outskirts of Salzburg, Castle Frohnburg shot to fame in the 1960s as the Von Trapp family villa in the movie, “The Sound of Music.” The bright yellow façade, gated entrance and scenic tree-line access road provided an elegant depiction of the family’s country estate in five scenes. When Maria (Julie Andrews) sings “I Have Confidence,” she makes her way along Frohnburg’s yellow wall before being awestruck at the iron gates and rushing across the entry courtyard.

Built in the late 1600s, Castle Frohnburg was used by counts and barons as one of the many country estates built just outside of Salzburg. After World War II, it was confiscated by the U.S. government, but later acquired by the Republic of Austria. Since then, it has been used by the Mozarteum University as the location of the Orff Institute for the study of elemental music & dance. It is not open to the public, but you can walk Maria’s path along Hellbrunner Allee to the gates at number 53.
Front of Schloss Frohnburg (Luckyprof, CC BY-SA 3.0 AT <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/at/deed.en>, via Wikimedia Commons)
**Prague Castle, Czechia**
The Prague Castle complex, or Pražský hrad, sits atop a steep hill and the many stairways on its western edge were used for multiple scenes in “Spider-Man: Far From Home” when Peter (Tom Holland) and his class visit Prague. Later in the film, Peter and MJ (Zendaya) share a charged moment on the beautiful stone Charles Bridge that connects the city’s old town section with the castle-side of the Vitava River. “Mission Impossible: Ghost Protocol” was also filmed at Prague Castle. In the film, Ethan Hunt (Tom Cruise) and Benji Dunn (Simon Pegg) sneak into the Kremlin and pass through a courtyard, two severely stark rooms and an ornate hall. In reality, these were all filmed inside the Prague Castle.
According to the Guinness Book of World Records, Prague Castle is the largest castle complex in the world. It was first built in 880 and became a seat of power for princes, kings and, later, Holy Roman Emperors. It is currently the official residence of the Czech president. A walled village grew below the castle, which is connected to the old town of Prague via the Charles Bridge. Like Peter and MJ, you can walk across the bridge and explore the Prague Castle grounds. There are also ticketed options, so you don’t need to sneak around like Ethan Hunt to enter the castle buildings and exhibitions.
View across Charles Bridge to the Prague Castle ()
**Doune Castle, Scotland**

This Scottish castle has been in many films and shows, but it was “Monty Python and the Holy Grail” that put it on the film industry map. Originally it was one of many castles slated for filming, but when the National Trust for Scotland revoked their permission for all but Doune, it became the filming location for nearly all the castle scenes in the movie. It was later used as Winterfell in the “Game of Thrones” pilot episode and Castle Leoch in the “Outlander” series.
Doune Castle is now maintained by Historical Environment Scotland as a tourist destination, and tickets can booked online at historicenvironment.scot. You can explore on your own, pretend to heckle the guards or present your own Trojan rabbit at the front gate, dance with the knights in the great hall, or escape temptation in the kitchens like our favorite Monty Python actors.
Duone Castle Exterior ()
**Castello Tramontano, Italy**
This Italian filming site is not simply the Castello (castle) Tramontano, but also the entire ancient town (Sassi) of Matera that stair-steps down the hills below it. The ancient look of the slightly unkempt stone buildings stacked upon each other has been used in many films set in biblical landscapes. It is where Jesus (Jim Caviezel) carries his cross and is crucified in “The Passion of the Christ,” it doubles for Bethlehem in “The Nativity Story” and, most recently, is a stand-in for Jerusalem in “The Book of Clarence.”
Castello construction began in 1501 by the Count of Matera to assert feudal control, but he was assassinated by overtaxed and disgruntled townsfolk in 1514 and the castle was left to ruin. It is still closed for repairs that began in 2008. The town below the castle is largely made of cave-dwellings dug into the hillside which are reported to have been occupied since the Paleolithic. The deep interiors are not apparent from the stacked house-like exteriors, a look that helped to create the town of Themyscira in “Wonder Woman.” The tiny streets were also subject to the opening shot car chase in the James Bond film “No Time to Die.” You can visit Matera, stay in a cave house hotel and wander the streets in the footsteps of Daniel Craig and Gal Gadot, up the winding stairs and alleyways for a view from the Castello Tramontano.

Segovia - Spain
The Alcázar of Segovia (literally, Segovia Castle) is the **Most Beautiful Castles in Europe**. It is a stone fortification, located in the old city of Segovia, Spain.
Rising out on a rocky crag above the confluence of the rivers Eresma and Clamores near the Guadarrama mountains, it is **one of the most distinctive castle-palaces in Spain** by virtue of its shape – like the bow of a ship.

In Love with the Wind – the castle with the magnificent structures made of marble and metamorphosed limestone from the fairy tales of a talented architect and dreamer, Georgi Tumpalov, is not only one of the **Best Castles in Europe**, it is the only newly built castle in Europe.
The Castle In Love with the Wind – a fairy tale near the sea.The place where the Castle is built is a unique natural phenomenon. Here, the wind loves the sun and always when the sun shines, there is a wind.
On this bare field near the village, Georgi Tumpalov, an architect and developer, decided to make it child’s dream come true – to build a castle that exists only in fairy tales. But a dream never comes alone. Tumpalov attracted to the modest village of Ravadinovo, standing 6 km from Sozopol, enormous crowds of visitors from all over the world. The castle was awarded the prize for the most attractive tourist site of the year by the Bulgarian Hotel and Restaurant Association. In 2013, Walt Disney used its natural décor to make its movie the Sleeping Beauty. Seven weeks after the death of King Ludwig II in 1886, Neuschwanstein Castle, one of the **Most Visited Castles in Europe,**was opened to the public.
The shy king had built the castle in order to withdraw from public life – now vast numbers of people came to view his private refuge.
Today Neuschwanstein is **one of the most popular of all the palaces and castles in Europe**. Every year 1.4 million people visit "the castle of the fairy-tale king". In the summer around 6,000 visitors a day stream through rooms that were intended for a single inhabitant.

This early 16th century **castle** is not only one of the **Best Castles in Europe**, it is one of Northern Ireland's iconic ruined castles.

Founded in the 10th century by Odo I, Count of Blois, it has had a turbulent history.
